
# Data and measurement {#sec-data}

Four sources enter the confirmatory analysis: the Anthropic Economic Index (AEI) releases, the O\*NET task and occupation files, the Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS), and the Kenneth French data library. Two further sources are descriptive or exploratory: the "could" exposure benchmarks used in RQ2 and the SEC EDGAR filings used for H6. The tables in this section come from the data audit, which reports coverage, missingness and measurement regimes only and relates no delegation measure to any outcome. The raw files, their retrieval times and their hashes are listed in @sec-app-replication.

## The AEI releases

AEI publishes aggregated, privacy-filtered counts of Claude conversations classified to O\*NET task statements, with the share in each collaboration pattern [@handa2025economic; @appel2025uneven; @appel2026economic; @massenkoff2026learning; @anthropic2026economicindex]. This paper uses all six releases published before the pre-registration: r1 on {{< var design.release.r1 >}}, r2 on {{< var design.release.r2 >}}, r3 on {{< var design.release.r3 >}}, r4 on {{< var design.release.r4 >}}, r5 on {{< var design.release.r5 >}} and r6 on {{< var design.release.r6 >}}. @tbl-releases gives each release's publication date, source, data window, geography levels and taxonomies. Two sources appear: `claude_ai`, the consumer product, in every release, and `1p_api`, Anthropic's first-party API, from r3 onwards. The r1 and r2 data windows are marked as defaults in @tbl-releases, because their repository files state no window and the dates come from the release reports. The r3 to r5 windows are single weeks as published, and r6 covers two calendar months. Geography is global in r1 and r2; from r3 the `claude_ai` files add countries and subregions.

{{< include _generated/tables/releases.md >}}

The releases arrive in three file layouts. The r1 and r2 files are separate tables keyed by task name. The r3 to r5 files share a facet layout, one row per value with its geography, platform, facet and variable. The r6 files are calendar-month extracts in a long metric layout that adds published SOC occupation rows and the O\*NET work-activity hierarchy.

The unit of observation throughout is a conversation, classified by a model and matched to a task. {{< var meta.wording >}} When later sections speak of delegation by task, occupation, industry or country, they mean the share of matched conversations in the automation patterns, weighted as stated, and nothing about the people who hold those occupations.

## Measurement regimes

@tbl-regimes (@sec-app-supplementary) lists, for each release and source, the platform scope, the classifier, the collaboration taxonomy, the suppression construct and the occupation basis; the decisions that follow from it are in the pre-analysis plan (@sec-app-pap). Four regime changes matter.

The first is platform scope. The consumer scope widens from the Free and Pro plans to include Max and then, in r6, the Cowork product; the API source enters at r3, and r6's API scope excludes Claude Code (@tbl-regimes; @sec-app-supplementary). The second is the classifier. No release file names the model that assigns conversations to tasks and patterns, so a change of classifier cannot be observed in the data and cannot be separated from a change in behaviour. The third is the collaboration taxonomy. Release r1 uses the earlier taxonomy, `collab_v1`, and publishes only an overall split, with no task-level patterns; r2 to r6 use `collab_v2`, with the same five pattern labels throughout. Following the AEI definition, automation is the sum of the `directive` and `feedback_loop` patterns and augmentation the sum of `task_iteration`, `validation` and `learning`. Both are renormalised over classified conversations, so the primary delegation measure, `automation_pct`, is defined identically in every release from r2 to r6 (D1).

The fourth is suppression. AEI withholds cells below its privacy thresholds, and the way it does so changes twice (@tbl-regimes; @sec-app-supplementary). In r2 each task carries a `filtered` share, and the patterns are renormalised over the remainder. In r3 to r5, small task-by-pattern cells are folded into a `not_classified` row alongside a `none` row. In r6 cells below the thresholds are simply absent, there is no `not_classified` row, and the patterns are published as shares of all conversations, which this paper renormalises. The base of classified conversations therefore differs between r2 and the later releases, and task-level pattern completeness is not comparable between r3 to r5 and r6. These changes bound what the trend hypothesis can show: H2 measures the change in measured within-task automation, which includes any change of platform, classifier or suppression, and @sec-rq1 reports it with that qualification. The occupation basis changes as well: r1 to r5 occupations are derived from task usage, while r6 publishes SOC occupation rows directly, which this paper uses for r6 (D9).

## The harmonised panel

The parsers write one long table indexed by release, period, source, geography, taxonomy, node and metric, with one value per cell. The panel keeps the distinction between a value that is unpublished and a value that is zero. A cell AEI does not publish has no row; it is never set to zero, and no later step fills it. A group of shares that sums to less than the whole is recorded as unpublished mass, not as a measured absence of usage. Data-quality checks run in code: shares may not exceed the whole within a node and geography beyond a fixed tolerance, task and occupation codes must be valid against the O\*NET and SOC lists, and the row count of each release is pinned. The zero assignment in the industry indices, discussed below, is the one place where unpublished occupations are given a value.

## Tasks, occupations and the O\*NET-SOC harmonisation

AEI identifies tasks by their statement text. Each statement is linked to an O\*NET Task ID through the O\*NET {{< var vintage.onet.primary >}} task file [@onet2025database], the earlier statements shipped with r2 and the O\*NET occupation crosswalk, and every occupation code is resolved to the O\*NET-SOC {{< var vintage.onet_soc >}} taxonomy, the vintage of the OEWS weights and of AEI's own r6 occupation rows. Some statements carry more than one candidate Task ID. Such a statement is allocated to the union of its candidates' occupations, and a task shared by several occupations gives each an equal part of its usage (D4). The equal split conserves usage and uses no employment information, so the numerator of the usage intensity defined below stays independent of its denominator. Its cost is that occupations sharing many statements can differ widely in intensity for reasons of allocation alone. An employment-proportional split is pre-registered as robustness row R11 (@sec-robustness).

## OEWS weights and the timing of the inputs

Occupation weights come from OEWS {{< var vintage.oews.primary >}} [@bls2025oews], at national level for each occupation's share of employment and at four-digit NAICS level for each industry's occupation mix. AEI occupations are joined to OEWS detailed codes by exact match, by rollup to the OEWS aggregate where OEWS publishes only the aggregate, and by a hybrid step for the codes that O\*NET-SOC splits and OEWS merges. Exact matching and rollup alone leave {{< var audit.unmatched_usage_pct >}} % of AEI usage without an OEWS occupation; after the hybrid step none is left, and the occupations AEI reaches hold {{< var audit.employment_covered_pct >}} % of OEWS employment. The remaining {{< var audit.oews_without_aei_emp_pct >}} % of employment sits in OEWS occupations with no AEI r6 occupation. Those occupations are unpublished in AEI, not measured as zero.

The timing of these inputs requires a correction to the design (PAP §10, S1). Design B, the confirmatory exposure vector, takes its AEI usage from release r2 alone, published on {{< var design.formation >}}, its formation date. Its OEWS {{< var vintage.oews.primary >}} weights were released on {{< var design.s1.oews_release >}}, after that formation date and inside the return window that opens on {{< var design.window.start >}}. Its task links come from O\*NET {{< var vintage.onet.primary >}}, which was also released after formation, although its task statements are byte-identical to those of O\*NET {{< var vintage.onet.r32 >}} (clarification C-74 on R32, @sec-app-deviations). Design B is therefore out of sample in its AEI data only; it is not strictly real-time in its occupation weights and task links (PAP §2.1). Both are slow-moving structural inputs that carry no return information, but the claim of real-time construction does not hold for them. Robustness row R32 rebuilds Design B from inputs public at formation, the OEWS {{< var vintage.oews.r32 >}} weights and the O\*NET {{< var vintage.onet.r32 >}} task file; since the task files are identical, R32 differs from the primary only in its weights. Row R1, which uses the OEWS {{< var vintage.oews.r1 >}} weights published during the return window, is labelled look-ahead wherever it appears. Both rows are reported in @sec-robustness and @sec-app-robustness-tables, and this timing caveat applies to every RQ2 correlation in @sec-rq2 and to every H5 and H5b number in @sec-markets.

## The industry crosswalk

The market tests use the {{< var design.n_industries >}} Fama–French industry portfolios (FF49), which are defined by SIC codes, while OEWS industries are NAICS codes. Each four-digit NAICS industry is mapped to SIC codes through the chain of Census concordances [@census2022concordances], and SIC codes are mapped to FF49 industries by the ranges of the French library's industry definitions. Where a NAICS code maps to several SIC codes, its employment is split equally among them (D23). This departs from the design specification, which called for an employment-weighted crosswalk. The departure is disclosed in PAP §10 and in @sec-app-deviations: the Census concordances carry no employment weights, and the equal split is the vector on which the power analysis was run and which was frozen at the tag. Its weights are therefore structural, not employment-based. The specification's employment-weighted crosswalk, which splits each NAICS industry in proportion to the employment of its finer NAICS children, is robustness row R33. The alternative many-to-one assignment, which gives each NAICS code wholly to one SIC code, is row R20 (@sec-robustness). Management of companies is excluded from FF49, because through holding-company SIC codes it would otherwise set the occupation mix of the finance industry (D7); row R15 redistributes it in proportion to mapped private employment. @tbl-audit-exposure-coverage (@sec-app-supplementary) reports, by design, the range and median of the share of each industry's employment that carries a delegation value.

## The exposure indices

The exposure indices follow the design specification as frozen in the pre-analysis plan (PAP §2.1). For occupation $o$, let $s_o$ be its share of AEI usage, $\pi_o$ its share of national employment, and $a_o$ and $g_o$ the automation and augmentation shares of its classified conversations. Usage, delegation and augmentation intensity are

$$
U_o = \frac{s_o}{\pi_o}, \qquad D_o = U_o \, a_o, \qquad A_o = U_o \, g_o .
$$

For industry $j$, with $e_{oj}$ the employment of occupation $o$ in $j$ and $\mathcal{O}_j$ the occupations of $j$ that carry a value, the industry index for each intensity $X \in \{U, D, A\}$ is the employment-weighted sum

$$
E^{X}_{j} = \sum_{o \in \mathcal{O}_j} w_{oj} \, X_o, \qquad w_{oj} = \frac{e_{oj}}{\sum_{o'} e_{o'j}} .
$$

Each index is standardised across the $J$ industries present, where $J$ = {{< var design.n_industries >}}:

$$
z^{X}_{j} = \frac{E^{X}_{j} - \bar{E}^{X}}{\sigma^{X}}, \qquad \bar{E}^{X} = \frac{\sum_{k} E^{X}_{k}}{J},
$$

with $\sigma^{X}$ the population standard deviation of $E^{X}$ across those industries (divisor $J$). The three standardised indices are `z_usage`, `z_delegation` and `z_augmentation`; H5 uses `z_delegation`, and H5b adds the AIOE benchmark beside it (@sec-methods).

Three exposure vectors are built from these formulas. Design B uses release r2 alone (`claude_ai`, the only r2 source) and is the confirmatory vector. `A_r2` is numerically the same vector, labelled exploratory because it serves the exploratory Design A analyses. `A_pooled` averages r2 to r6 `claude_ai` with equal release weights; it uses releases published during and after the return window, so it contains look-ahead and is labelled so wherever it appears (PAP §10, S3). @tbl-audit-exposure-coverage (@sec-app-supplementary) shows that the Design B `z_delegation` distribution is strongly right-skewed: its largest value, for {{< var audit.exposure.b.z_del_max_industry >}}, is {{< var audit.exposure.b.z_del_max >}} SD, against {{< var audit.exposure.b.z_del_2nd >}} SD for the next industry. @sec-methods explains how row R12, which uses standardised ranks, and row R13, which drops that industry, enter the confirmatory reporting.

## The zero-assignment assumption

An OEWS occupation with no AEI usage enters the indices with $U_o$, $D_o$ and $A_o$ set to zero (D3). This is an assumption, not a measurement. AEI leaves these occupations unpublished; it does not report that their conversations number zero. Under Design B, occupations holding {{< var audit.zero_assigned_pct.b >}} % of OEWS employment are unpublished in r2 and assigned zero by assumption; the share is the same for `A_r2` ({{< var audit.zero_assigned_pct.a_r2 >}} %). Under `A_pooled`, which draws on more releases and so matches more tasks, the share unpublished and assigned zero by assumption is {{< var audit.zero_assigned_pct.a_pooled >}} %. These figures measure something different from the {{< var audit.oews_without_aei_emp_pct >}} % of employment with no AEI r6 occupation: that share refers to r6's published occupations, while Design B rests on r2, which matches fewer tasks (PAP §10, S5). The occupations concerned are mostly hands-on trades (D3). Dropping them instead would treat their unpublished usage as equal to their industry's mean, which would overstate exposure in the industries that employ them most. Robustness row R3 drops them from the industry sums (@sec-robustness). The RQ2 correlations depend on this choice, and R3 is the row that lowers them most (@sec-rq2).

## The "could" benchmarks

RQ2 compares the observed indices with two measures of what language models could do. The AI Occupational Exposure index (AIOE) of @felten2021occupational [@aioe2021data] is published on SOC codes of an earlier vintage. It is carried to O\*NET-SOC {{< var vintage.onet_soc >}} through the O\*NET occupation crosswalk: an earlier code takes the successors of all its O\*NET children, a split copies the value and a merge takes the simple mean (D6). Its weakness is that some earlier codes are copied to several successors with different content. The published BLS SOC crosswalk [@bls2018soccrosswalk], with the same copy and mean rule, is robustness row R14. The second benchmark is the occupation-level exposure of @eloundou2024gpts [@openai2023gptsdata], already on O\*NET-SOC codes. Its headline rating is the human annotators' β, chosen because it does not depend on a language model's assessment of language-model exposure; the GPT-4 β of that study (`dv_rating_beta`) is reported beside it in every RQ2 table (D8), and row R17 makes it the headline. Both benchmarks are descriptive (@sec-rq2) and enter no confirmatory test, except that AIOE is the control in H5b.

The benchmarks pass through the same OEWS weights, the same crosswalk and the same standardisation as the AEI indices, giving `z_aioe`, `z_eloundou` and `z_eloundou_gpt4`. Since both sides of every RQ2 comparison inherit the same occupation-to-industry weights, part of any correlation between them reflects the shared occupational mix of industries rather than agreement between "could" and "does" at the occupation level. RQ2 reports Spearman rank correlations across the industries, with confidence intervals from an industry bootstrap of {{< var rq2.n_draws >}} draws under the project seed {{< var design.seed >}} (@sec-rq2).

## Market data

Industry returns are the French library's daily value-weighted FF49 portfolio returns, and the factors are the five Fama–French factors and momentum [@french2026datalibrary; @fama2015five; @carhart1997persistence]. French revises these files retroactively, so only the frozen files whose hashes are listed in @sec-app-replication are used. The market-data end date is frozen at {{< var design.window.end >}}, the last date of the frozen daily files, which is also the end of the confirmatory return window that opens on {{< var design.window.start >}}, a span of {{< var design.window.months >}} months. The pre-registration was frozen, as tag {{< var pap.tag >}}, before any code read an industry return dated on or after the seal date, {{< var design.seal_date >}} (@sec-app-disclosures); the history before the seal supplies the null scale described in @sec-methods.

## Filings for the talk index

H6, which is exploratory, compares how often firms in an industry mention AI in their 10-K filings with the industry's AEI usage exposure. Its data come from SEC EDGAR [@sec2026edgar]. For each industry the talk index is the share of distinct 10-K filers whose 10-K filed in {{< var h6.talk.year >}}, between {{< var h6.talk.filed_start >}} and {{< var h6.talk.filed_end >}} and so before Design B's formation date, is returned by EDGAR full-text search for at least one primary term of the pre-registered AI dictionary (D12). The denominator is the count of filers of the same forms in the EDGAR full index. Two inputs are fixed at retrieval, not at the filing year. Each filer's industry is its current SIC code in the EDGAR submissions file (C-40), retrieved at {{< var h6.vintage.submissions_retrieved_utc >}} and applied to every filing year; and the numerator uses the phrase matching of the SEC's full-text search as implemented on the retrieval date (PAP §6). Filers whose SIC falls in no FF49 range are left unmapped and reported, never assigned to an industry. All H6 results are reported as exploratory in @sec-markets.
